extracted.intended_audience: OSHA stakeholders: employers, workers, occupational safety and health professionals, researchers, and other commenters on the OSHA heat NPRM
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and commenting on OSHA's proposed heat standard (NPRM) including the scientific evidence, risk assessment methods, incidence estimates, and proposed definitions/criteria for heat-related injuries and illness. Intended for stakeholders submitting data, analyses, or comments to OSHA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a heat-related injury
rubrics_metrics.description: A heat-related injury means an injury, such as a fall or cut, that is linked to heat exposure. A heat-related injury may occur as a result of a heat-related illness, such as a fracture following heat syncope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to classify injuries as heat-related when there is a link to heat exposure; examples include injuries resulting from impaired balance or psychomotor performance due to heat. No single ICD or OIICS code exists specifically for heat-related injuries, so clinicians/researchers may combine a heat-related illness code with other injury codes to indicate heat attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion criteria for heat-related illness/injury (data relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA's inclusion criteria for HRIs in surveillance data are cases involving days away from work, workers' compensation claims, emergency department visits, or inpatient hospitalization—demonstrating that the HRIs are a material impairment of health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA relied on such sources to demonstrate extent of risk; these criteria define which cases are sufficiently severe to count in incidence estimates used in the risk assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation for coding of heat-attributed injuries in datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: An injury specifically attributed to heat would be expected to be assigned both a heat-related OIICS or ICD code and an injury OIICS or ICD code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because no single dedicated ICD/OIICS code exists for all heat-related injuries, researchers can indicate heat attribution by combining heat-related codes (e.g., 'Effects of heat and light') with injury event/nature codes. OSHA references relevant OIICS event code 531 and ICD/nature codes (e.g., 172-*, ICD-9 992.0-992.9) as pertinent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and limits of surveillance data (BLS SOII) for incidence estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: BLS Survey of Occupational Injuries and Illnesses (SOII) is the primary nationwide source for nonfatal occupational injury/illness surveillance; BLS uses full-time equivalent denominators (2,000 hours = 1 FTE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SOII estimates count heat-related cases coded as 'Exposure to environmental heat' (event code 531) and 'Effects of heat and light' (nature codes 172-). OSHA notes SOII incidence rates may underestimate risk among heat-exposed workers because BLS denominators include many unexposed workers (e.g., office workers), diluting rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to accurately estimate denominator (number of heat-exposed workers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimating annual incidence among heat-exposed workers requires accurately estimating the number of exposed workers; using a larger denominator that includes unexposed workers dilutes incidence estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA flags lack of a published estimate for the number of U.S. workers exposed to hazardous heat and treats many surveillance-based incidence estimates as lower bounds. Commenters should provide better exposure-denominator data where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of stratified or cohort incidence estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidence estimates stratified by sector, industry, or occupation, or cohort studies where the entire cohort is presumed heat-exposed, provide more accurate estimates of risk among heat-exposed workers than whole-workforce surveillance estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA considers sector/industry-stratified workers' compensation data and cohort-based incidence as helpful; these often yield higher (and likely more accurate) incidence rates because their denominators better reflect exposed populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological note on case-crossover and time-varying confounders
rubrics_metrics.description: Case-crossover studies use cases as their own controls and can control for time-invariant confounders (age, sex, race), but they remain vulnerable to time-varying confounders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of potential time-varying confounders include air pollutants (e.g., ozone) and sleep duration influenced by nighttime temperatures. Risk assessments relying on such studies should consider these limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification methods for heat-related claims in workers' compensation data
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers may identify heat-related workers' compensation claims using coding on claims (e.g., ANSI Z16.2 codes), ICD codes (e.g., ICD-9 992.0-992.9), and physician review to remove miscoded or irrelevant cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA summarizes the Washington State study (Bonauto et al., 2007) which used ANSI Z16.2 and ICD-9 codes and physician review; researchers should document code sets and case-review processes when estimating incidence from compensation data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat-related mechanisms: impaired psychomotor performance (movement/strength/coordination/fatigue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat exposure can impair psychomotor function—movement, strength, coordination—leading to fatigue that compromises performance and can precipitate injuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms include central and peripheral fatigue from heat strain (e.g., metabolic changes, lactate accumulation). OSHA cites surveys and studies showing fatigue increases with rising heat exposure and that fatigue can trigger safety risks (not following procedures, distraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat-related mechanisms: impaired postural stability and balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat exposure and dehydration can impair postural stability and balance via negative neuromuscular effects, increasing injury risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence includes studies showing hypohydration plus heat leads to decreased neuromuscular control and poorer gait/technique; combined exertion, dehydration, and heat can dilute blood sodium and lead to severe outcomes (pulmonary congestion, cerebral effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat-related mechanisms: impaired accuracy, speed, and reaction time
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat strain can compromise accuracy, speed, and reaction time; effects vary with severity of heat strain and task complexity (sometimes faster but less accurate responses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies report decrements on mathematical/reaction-time tasks at high ambient temperatures (e.g., ~32.2°C with ~15% average performance decrement). Occupational studies show worse reaction time and more errors at WBGTs in higher ranges (examples cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat-related mechanisms: impaired mental/cognitive performance (including thresholds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat exposure can impair cognition (memory, attention, information processing), visual-motor tracking, decision-making, and judgment, all increasing injury risk; some effects occur well below physiological tolerance limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA cites evidence of increased unsafe behaviors above ~23°C WBGT and cognitive/psychological declines at temperatures in the 27–33°C range depending on task complexity and exposure duration; core temperatures of ~38°C can begin to show changes, with more severe changes near 40°C. For acclimatized workers continuously working 4 hours, suggested limits in cited study: ≤31.1°C (hot-humid) and ≤32.2°C (hot-desert).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observed temperature–injury associations and magnitudes (epidemiologic findings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epidemiologic studies report associations between higher ambient/heat metrics and increased traumatic injury risk and overall injury counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: humidex above 25°C (77°F) was associated with increased traumatic injuries among agricultural workers; increasing average daily mean WBGT above 30°C (86°F) was associated with higher injury risk (Guatemala sugarcane harvesters, though not always statistically significant); California study estimated ~20,000 additional injuries/year between 2001–2018 related to hotter temperatures with injury risk increases of 5–7% at 85–90°F and 10–15% above 100°F compared to days in the 60s°F.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other factors contributing to heat-related injury risk (PPE, vision, dexterity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional contributors include PPE that insulates or prevents evaporative cooling (e.g., self-contained breathing apparatus, impermeable reflective vests, non-ventilated helmets), fogged safety glasses or sweat impairing vision, and sweaty palms reducing dexterity and tool control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA provides examples and study findings: inside-helmet temperatures can exceed ambient by >20°C, leading workers to remove PPE and exposing to other hazards; surveys report fogged safety glasses and loss of tool control as frequent causes of heat-related injuries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance for commenters: provide data, citations, and reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA requests stakeholders provide relevant data, information, or additional studies (or citations) supporting their view, and explain the reasoning for including such studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When submitting comments, stakeholders should supply underlying data and an explanation of why the studies/data are relevant to OSHA's conclusions about heat-related health effects, including methodological details that support inclusion or critique (e.g., exposure definitions, denominators, coding methods).
